utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler. Welcome back again. I know it's boring, but I have to remind you again that you have to tell the truth. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We left off yesterday just as we were about to show a video-clip. May there be peace in this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] and I wish a comfortable stay and a pleasant stay to Mr. Butler here amongst us here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the second video clip, namely P2125. The footage has to do with the abuse of convoys in Ilidza. It is 1D217.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] At the Ilidza check-point the Serbian army discovered 24.500 bullets in United Nations trucks authorised to transport humanitarian aid to Muslims in Hrasnica. "A convoy transporting humanitarian aid from the airport to Butmir in Hrasnica was stopped today in Ilidza. Following a routine check by the Ilidza military police members, it was discovered that the container with flour had a false bottom with steel boxes. This was a good enough reason to question the regularity of the convoy. "Members of the French Battalion who were escorting the convoy were not able to tell us what was in the bunkers beneath the containers. "The convoy was held up, members of UNPROFOR, the UNHCR and police were called and, in their presence the check was carried out. The containers were off-loaded from the trucks, and with the help of a crane, the upper part of the containers were detached from the platform to which they were attached. "Journalist: Mr. Popovic, the check is now complete, tell us what have you discovered in the trucks transporting humanitarian aid to Hrasnica. "Mr. Popovic: Found in the trucks which left for Hrasnica this morning at 0945 hours were 5.000 rounds of 12.7 ammunition and 19.540 rounds of 7.9 sniper ammunition. They were discovered, as you could see for yourself, in the false bottom under the containers. This is the second time that we have found aid for the Muslim forces' side, in weapons and ammunition in the humanitarian aid in the area of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade. "Journalist: Did you see whose ammunition it is? Do you know where is it from? "Mr. Popovic: All the ammunition was produced in Konjic and was transported by air to the Sarajevo airport and then by land. On this occasion, it was being transported and escorted by the French forces and this is the quantity of ammunition that was discovered. "We asked for official information from the gentleman from the UN, but we got none because, as they explained to us, they are not authorised to give information. "In an informal conversation with an UNHCR representative we were told that they have nothing to do with the trucks or containers and that they were responsible solely for the load being transported in the containers and they are not interested in what is under the containers. "The representatives of the Foreign Legion excused themselves by saying that they only escorted the convoy and the UN police claimed that they would examine the case and inform us of the results as soon as possible. "Right now, we do not yet know who loaded the trucks at the airport and where the ammunition was loaded. We do not know what is happening with the checks at the airport and how many such convoys have gone past. But one thing is certain and that is that this is the umpteenth time that we see UNPROFOR is transporting and distributing weapons and ammunition to the Muslims under the guys of humanitarian aid."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just one clarification. You gave us the number of this video. It is P -- one moment. P2125, and then you added another number, 1D217. Is that the same video -- is it the 65 ter number of the same video or is it the transcript? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, 1D217 is merely the transcript of the video. When uploading the surrogate sheet for the video footage, we saw the OTP omitted to upload the transcript as well. We have had it from before and that is the number it was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That clarifies the situation. Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now show D281 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case, I would like to ask you if you are tendering the transcript of the video we have seen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With your leave, yes, we tender these into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to suggest that the transcripts be assigned the corresponding P number of the footage and then, perhaps, with the addition of an A at the end so as to avoid a situation where the video-clip itself would bear an assigned number and its corresponding transcript a different number. Or perhaps we should merely ask the Prosecution that the OTP should, in addition to the surrogate sheet, also upload the transcript of the video footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I was just wondering if it's possible for the Defence to give the date of the incident that has been shown on video-clip, unless it would become apparent subsequently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Nyambe. We will do our best to attach a date to it, but we do have original documents indicating when it happened. Can we have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure if it's D or P78.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with yesterday's video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The date is the command of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, the 8th of June, 1995. This command reports to the Drina Corps the incident that we just discussed. Under 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, let me interrupt you for a moment before you go ahead. Is it D78 or P78?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D78.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And after conferring with Mr. Registrar, the transcript of the last video will be attached to P2125 so that we have only one document with this number. That means it's not a separate document but attached to the video itself. Now, you may go ahead, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At the Rogatica check-point, the Ukrainian convoy comprising three vehicles went past. "A UNHCR convoy from Karakaj to Zepa, which arrived at the check-point yesterday, is still in Rogatica because on the earlier day a certain amount of ammunition was found in the convoy." So the date is the 7th of June, 1995. That is the date which is the date of the incident of yesterday's video footage. As for today's footage, my legal assistant will let you know the exact date it has been mentioned within this news report broadcast on TV.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please bear in mind that D78 is the document underpinning the video footage of yesterday in terms of the date. We now have a document of an attempt to prevent the smuggling of fuel in convoys. It's a document that relates to the UNHCR, UNPROFOR, and international organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, and I apologise but it is not clear to us if the video P2145 or these -- are both these transcripts from that same video or different? 1D217 is one transcript and 1D234 is the other transcript. Are they both from video P2145? That's a little unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic. Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as for P2145, the transcript is 1D217. This is -- as for yesterday's video, P2126, the transcript of that video-clip is 1D234.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't know if that is a slip of the tongue. Mr. McCloskey and you, you mentioned P2145. I thought we have seen P2125. Please clarify that. Mr. Gajic, you should not always follow Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I misread it, perhaps. No. Video is P12 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Gajic repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are going to have an additional problem. Please repeat the number correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat it all. The video footage P2125 has the corresponding transcript 1D217.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, video P2126 has the corresponding transcript 1D234.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am not sure if that was already decided yesterday, but the latter transcript will be attached to P2126. I hope that clarifies the situation. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that all fits. Ms. Stewart and Mr. Gajic are all on the right page and we all made a few little mistakes but that's now just right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was a really difficult exercise. Mr. Tolimir, please continue, and bear in mind that we have Mr. Butler here to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we show D281, a document regarding the smuggling of fuel in the UNPROFOR and UNHCR vehicles. Thank you. We have the document before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's issued by the command of the 1st Birac Infantry Brigade, dated the 12th of May, 1995, signed by commander Colonel Svetozar Andric. If we scroll down we will see it, Svetozar Andric. In paragraph 1 he writes: "We have received information that members of the UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and other international organisations have been transporting fuel illegally to Muslims in the enclaves of Sarajevo, Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. "They smuggle fuel in double or large tanks on combat and noncombat vehicles which they empty in the enclaves, leaving just the quantity needed for their return journey from the enclaves to the territory of the FRY or Republika Srpska." And his order is: "Train and prepare personnel at the check-point in the area of Crni Vrh," that's his area of responsibility, "with a view to international representatives of UNHCR, UNPROFOR and others past these checkpoints." Under 2: "Check combat and noncombat vehicles thoroughly in order to measure accurately the quantities of fuel in their double and basic tanks and other secret storage places." I will not be reading through the rest. Mr. Butler, did you read any document either by the UNHCR or the VRS or do you have any other knowledge about fuel being smuggled in hidden storage tanks or double storage tanks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, good morning. I am generally aware from my research that the VRS believed that fuel was being smuggled in in both ways that are depicted in this particular report. One of them was that fuel was being potentially smuggled in through hidden or secret tanks on various vehicles. The second was a practice where vehicles would be travelling to the enclaves with full fuel tanks in excess of what they might be expected to actually consume in a one-day trip back and forth to the enclaves, whichever enclave they were going to, and then in that enclave excess amounts of fuel would be drained out. So that was a concern that the VRS had, and again it's amply illustrated in this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Having viewed the two video-clips concerning the smuggling in Rogatica and Ilidza, can you tell me if the activities conducted by the UNHCR and UNPROFOR in smuggling ammunition, could they have remained unknown to the UNPROFOR since there was media coverage of it at the time and in view of the fact that protest letters were written as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to - again, I have not read UN reporting related to this issue - but I would have to assume that given the media coverage, and I am aware that the UN monitored the media reporting from the various parties, as well as complaints coming from the VRS, again I have to assume that the leadership of the UNPROFOR in Sarajevo was given notice of these allegations as well as provided proof by the VRS that such violations were occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, if this was the case, tell us: Did you come across any material dealing with investigations in the UNPROFOR and UNHCR because of the smuggling of weapons and fuel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not come across that material, but in fairness I didn't look for it. It may well be out there as part of the broader body of documents and information, but since that was not a particular focus of my research work with respect to Srebrenica, like I said, if I came across it it didn't register.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If both the VRS and you are ignorant of any measures that may have been taken against perpetrators of these activities, is it only justifiable for the VRS to carry out thorough checks in order to look for possible ammunition in goods such as flour, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, notwithstanding my particular ignorance on this issue, and as I have said, I believe a number of days, certainly by January of 1995 the VRS believed it had more than adequate cause to institute an inspections regime to ensure that these type of supplies, be it ammunition, be it extra fuel, was not going into the enclaves where it would be used for military purposes. And, in fact, they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Several days ago, you referred to directives 7 and 7(1) and I said that we would be discussing those later. You specifically quoted the portion of the directive as to what the prospects for future life in Srebrenica were, and this was mentioned in Directive 7 but not in Directive 7(1).

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at Directive 7, P1214, page 15 in Serbian and 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, while we wait for the next document to appear, I would like to come back on document P2125. This is the video footage that we have seen, and it deals with the smuggling of ammunition and weapons that were found in a container of the HCR, of the UNHCR, and in fact, I would like to mention or talk about all the other ammunition and weapons that had been discovered in other convoys. As far as you are concerned, and as far as you know, were investigations launched by the United Nations or by the local police in order to establish who was responsible for these types of acts? Were these individual actions from the drivers or the people who were transporting the goods? Or do you think that it might have been a deliberate action from the UNHCR or from other international organisations who were present on the ground? Because when we see document P2125, P2125, as I have said, and when we see that there was a false bottom in the container, one could think that it might not just be one driver or one person who was trying to hide these things. It might not be just one driver who manufactured this double-deck or false bottom. So I think that it might be important in order to understand the reaction of the of the VRS. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As evidenced and as you indicated in your question, and when one goes back to, I believe, yesterday morning when we were looking at a number of documents produced by General Tolimir relating to the situation in the smuggling of fuel and munitions into the Bihac enclave, it is clear that as a matter of policy within the Bosnian Muslim military forces and their political organs that there was an organised campaign in order to use whatever means necessary - and in this case it was through an international organisation - what they needed to do in order to smuggle weapons, smuggle ammunition, and other military supplies, to isolated military forces, many of whom can only be accessed by the United Nations because of their presence in safe areas in or other surrounded areas. Obviously when one looks at those documents relating to Bihac, the reports make it clear that the UNHCR is not a witting partner, they don't know that they are being used for this purpose, although certainly some individuals within the UNHCR organisation at some level have to be complicit in this, but certainly the organisation does not seem to be aware of it. I assume the UN did investigations when these issues were brought to their attention, but I am not aware of the details of them. So, I mean, we are back to the similar situation, whether organizationally the United Nations was complicit in the efforts to bring ammunition or whether, just like in any other organisation, elements within the organisation were corrupted by the various parties for their various reasons, and coerced or encouraged or bribed to take part in these smuggling activities. But without having a detailed knowledge of the investigations and any results received, I don't know that I can answer the question any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You have, indeed, answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just want a bit of clarification on your part of your answer in line 14, where you say: "The UNHCR is not a witting partner." Can you elaborate on that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My -- the information that I have and that I believe is that, as an entire organisation, the UNHCR in Bosnia was not a voluntary participant in a process which would smuggle ammunition to various warring parties. It obviously would fly directly against their mandated charter. However, clearly within the UNHCR organisation in Bosnia as well as in other parts that were Serbian Bosnia, individual members or groups of members had been bribed or otherwise coopted by ABiH military or civilian bodies into this effort for whatever reason they were doing it. I suspect the short answer is it was profitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we are now looking at Directive 7. The relevant page with information about the Drina Corps. Could we scroll down to see the Drina Corps in English? Thank you. It says: "With the daily planned combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." I'm sorry, I started reading before saying that this is in line 5 from the top through line 9. So if you all found it ... My question is: As you have studied this thoroughly, is the same assignment given in Directive 7(1)?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the language in Directive 7(1) does not quote this passage verbatim, it is a more technical accounting or recounting of the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case let's look first at the heading of this Directive 7(1) to see that it's a document from the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see the last page of this directive. Last page says Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I heard that this was referred to as Directive 7(1) and of course this is Directive 7. That's, of course, an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed we have now Directive 7. This is P214 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now play Directive 7(1) as well. That's P2196, to compare both paragraphs for the headings and the signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a mistake in the displaying of Directive 7(1).

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it just a technical mistake, a technical error in Directive 7(1)? Is there a single word of creating unbearable conditions like in Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think you should check the number of the document you are asking for.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We've just checked. I called the wrong number. P119 should be Directive 7(1). 1199. We now see the Serbian version. We see that it's Directive 7(1), issued on 31st March, 1995. That's page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And we should now look at paragraph 3, the decision, or perhaps paragraph 4. No, it's paragraph 3 -- sorry, 5.3, both in Serbian and in English. Page 5. Paragraph 5.3. Here we see paragraph 5.3. It reads: "The Drina Corps: Prevent an enemy breakthrough along selected operative tactical axes with persistent defence and active combat actions on the north-west part of the front and around the enclaves and tie down as many enemy troops possible through diversionary -- through sabotage actions and operative tactical camouflage measures. "In co-operation with the Eastern Bosnian Corps, complete tasks from Operation Spreca 95 as soon as possible and break through in the first phase of the operation to the Vis-Kalesija line, then regroup forces and in the second and third phases of the operation in co-operation with forces of the Eastern Bosnian Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps, the air force, and air defence, by an appropriate manoeuvre, infiltrating strong groups into the enemy rear, and introducing strong armoured mechanised forces, execute an attack in the general direction of Kalesija-Dubrava-Tuzla, reaching as soon as possible the Serici village-Zivinice-Jasicak-Ravno hill line, thereby cutting off the forces of the 2nd Corps of the so-called BH army south of that line. Support from the air force and PVO." Is this a technical error --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down while reading. The court reporter can't follow at the same speed. Now your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, is this a technical error since Zepa and Srebrenica are not mentioned at all? Is there any reference to any attack on Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first answer is no, I do not believe this is a technical error at all. It is correct. There is not any specific language pertaining to an attack on Zepa and Srebrenica. What this document and this passage represents in more technical military terms than Directive 7 is not necessarily what is going to be accomplished from a broader perspective, but in this particular case, in more military terms, how it's going to be accomplished. What are specific articulatable objectives within a military planning and execution process. I would remind both you and the Court that the goal of Directive 7 was a document to be endorsed by the political leadership and the Supreme Command of the Republika Srpska. The members of the Supreme Command were not professional soldiers. They were civilians. Therefore, the language in Directive 7 had to at least be nontechnical so they could understand, in general terms, what the military was seeking to accomplish. Directive 7(1) is the amplification of Directive 7 and it is primarily designed to go to a military audience. As a result, you know, the text pertaining to these activities is for more technical in nature and ultimately would lead to those same results.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I am asking you: Does Directive 7 and Directive 7(1) make reference to these difficult conditions of life in Srebrenica. Is there any mention of it in Directive 7(1) written by the military leadership?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do Directive 7 or 7(1) mention any direct attack on Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. My understanding is that the guidance is to create the conditions to make life unbearable within the enclaves. It does not call for a direct military assault of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Main Staff transmit the message to its units that they should create such conditions through Directive 7(1) which relies on Directive 7? I am repeating the question, did the Main Staff in Directive 7(1), written based on Directive 7, tell the units to create difficult or unbearable conditions in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Directive 7(1) they did not use that language as a specific order to the units. It does not surprise me that they didn't use that language because from a military perspective, there is no direct military act that creates unbearable conditions. You -- in order to achieve that goal, you have to begin to issue a number of orders through a period of time which then are implemented by the military organs, and many of those acts, particularly with respect to the UNPROFOR, were not acts that could be directed by the specific corps. They were acts that had to be accomplished at the Main Staff level. So when you look at the language of 7(1) it specifically gives various corps orders --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Excuse me. While we are at this point, I asked you, did the Main Staff order them to create such conditions at all? Because we are dealing now with what the Main Staff did, and then we will discuss perhaps later whether other language was used somewhere else in Directive 7 to indicate that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to interrupting the witness. He was making a good-faith effort to answer that specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Butler to continue with his answer. The -- you see the beginning of the sentences: "So when you look at the language of 7(1), it specifically gives various corps orders ..." Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It specifically gives the various corps orders to attack on various lines of advance. It gives them specific objectives. It tells them specifically which units to co-ordinate with, and those are proper orders to give to subordinate military units; that is, terminology that they understand and the terminology that military professionals are trained to make supplemental plans for and operate under. The thing going back to the language between Directive 7 and Directive 7(1) is that had the language of Directive 7 - "create a situation that makes life unbearable in the enclaves" - been transmitted to the Drina Corps, as verbatim, the Drina Corps would have had a very broad list of questions back to the Main Staff asking just what that means and what you would want us to do. It's the same scenario, militarily speaking, that arguably the United Nations people in Srebrenica found themselves in. They had a very clear or very broad political mandate, but as military personnel, you know, they did not have clarifying data as exactly what that meant in missions that they were trained and capable of performing. So that's why I go back to the fact that 7(1) is a technical order which lays out a list of concrete military tasks to the Corps in a manner that they can understand and prepare for. Directive 7 is meant for a broader political and military audience that lays out the broader goals in terms that the civilian leadership understands and can endorse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question remains the same: Does Directive 7, yes or no, contain any reference, any word about creating unbearable conditions issued by the Main Staff to subordinate units? I apologise, I meant Directive 7(1). Directive 7 was issued by the Supreme Commander and Directive 7(1) by the Main Staff. Does Directive 7(1), issued by the Main Staff, contain a single word amounting to an on order to attack Zepa and Srebrenica and to create unbearable conditions there? Is there such an assignment given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness has answered this question already several times, but you may repeat your answer like Mr. Tolimir repeated his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, it does not, and it does not for the reasons that I have previously articulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I am happy the Trial Chamber understands. Little matter that I don't understand, because I am not the one who will make the judgement. So you say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's not a question of understanding. If you look back to page 17, lines 7 through 11, you asked: "Does Directive 7 and Directive 7(1) make reference to these difficult conditions of life in Srebrenica? Is there any mention of it in Directive 7(1) written by the military leadership?" The witness answered clearly: "No, sir." And all the other answers were his explanation why, about his understanding about the purpose of Directive 7(1). I think he has elaborated on that quite a lot. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am glad you have noted this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Does Directive 7, written by the Supreme Commander, order an attack on Zepa and Srebrenica? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to basically first say that I disagree with your assertion that Directive 7 was written by the Supreme Commander. It was not. Directive 7 was, as noted, drafted by General Milovanovic. It was forwarded to the Supreme Command for the approval ratification and signature of the Supreme Commander but that document was written by the Main Staff for the Supreme Commander. So having prefaced that, the next answer is my understanding is that the order to the Drina Corps is to create an unbearable situation. It does not call for a direct attack on Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If it doesn't call for a direct attack on Zepa and Srebrenica, do Directives 7 and 7(1) constitute a basis for an attack on Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is that those documents create or call for the creation of the climate necessary to eliminate the enclaves. It does not necessarily mean by physical attack. As I have testified previously, the VRS laid out that what they believe the best case scenario was going to be was that they could create such unbearable conditions that the UN would quit the enclaves and in essence take the civilian population out with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Could we just at this point ask Mr. Butler to clarify who he believes drafted Directive 7? He -- just so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He said that. And you may deal with that in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, concerning assignments from Directive 7, who is responsible? Is it only the signatory or can those who participated in the drafting of the directive also be responsible? I believe that's the answer that Mr. McCloskey wanted.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first off I can clarify I did misspeak. It's not General Milovanovic, it was General Miletic. Other at that time I believe it was still Colonel Miletic, the chief of operations of the Main Staff. Getting back to your question, obviously, Directive 7 was not drafted by -- it may be physically drafted by a single individual, but Directive 7 is going to be a compilation of the work of all of the organs of the Main Staff as they are the technical experts for the military. So it would be expected that for operational issues it would be then the chief of operations; for issues pertaining to intelligence and security, it would be assistant commander for intelligence and security; for logistics, it would be the assistant commander for logistics. So each various body of the Main Staff would have significant input into that document as they represented the military's technical experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Let me ask you again: We are in court, would every individual who placed as much as a comma in that directive be held accountable or responsible before a court of law, or would it be the person who authored the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Tolimir, this has to be answered and decided at the end of this trial by the Chamber. It's not for the witness to decide about personal responsibility, criminal responsibility for certain actions related to the indictment. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thought that we could hear the opinion of the expert because he did speak of responsibility, too, in his writing, but I do accept what you said. I have no difficulty with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, since these are strategic documents, do Directives 7 and 7(1) contain strategic objectives of the operations detailed within on a strategic level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If that is the case, can you tell us, then, based on the item which starts with words: "I hereby decide ..." What is the decision stated therein, to mount an attack on Srebrenica and Zepa, or to launch several operations, and if so, which and how many?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, could you refer me to where in the document you are discussing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me assist you in answering my question. There is a section which details the decision by the author, and it starts with the words: "I hereby decide ..." Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I am asking, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give the reference where that can be found in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's look at paragraph 4 of Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There we have it: "I have decided to:" This is something else. We are looking to read from directive 7, D1214. Let's see if the commander has decided which strategic operations need to be conducted and whether he assigned them names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give a clear reference. What document do you want to have on the screen and which paragraph you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have P1214 on our -- D1214 on our screens. And we need item 4 or paragraph 4. We have it. That's page 8 in English. Where it reads: "I hereby decide:"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Under 1: "Through a decisive Defence by the 30th Infantry Division, 22nd Infantry Brigade," et cetera, "and toward the Republic of Croatia forces, and by putting up a resolute defence in other sectors of the war front coupled with intensive operation on the segment of the front line within the areas of responsibilities of other corps, inflict on the enemy as much personnel, materiel, and equipment damage as possible," et cetera, "and by one to two strategic level operations with forces of up to corps strength." And then in the brackets we have the respective corps, Eastern Bosnia Corps, Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Herzegovina Corps, et cetera: "And three to four tactical level operations, advance as far as possible toward major enemy administrative and industrial centres, crush and destroy his forces, and thus create conditions for a triumphant end to the civilian war." And now he proceeded to define what the brunt of the activities of the Sarajevo Corps would be. Let me now reiterate my question. And you see the last line where he mentions the Drina Corps. We can read the entire thing. The last paragraph: "When carrying out strategic level operations, Operation Sadjestvo co-ordinated action 95 shall be carried out first, followed by Operation Prozor-95, Operation Spreca-95 is to take place in the run up to Operation Sadjestvo-95 and in the run-up to Operation Prozor-95, planned operations within the responsibility of the two corps will take place." This is my question: Did he define precisely which strategic operations need to be carried out on a strategic level and did he name them, too?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he laid out the broad strategic situation where he -- or where the Supreme Command in this case saw the strategic offensive and defensive activities, where they were going to take place, and laid out a number of strategic-level operations that would take place in time through the conduct of this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Quite apart from these operations, was it possible for anyone to do anything? Was it possible for someone to define what strategic operations are to be carried out and what they should be called and what areas they should cover?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, this being strategic guidance, the expectation was in not only Directive 7(1) but in supplemental orders that it would be the Main Staff who took these larger strategic objectives and turned them into military guidance for the execution by subordinate corps and other formations. So we weren't changing -- or they are not changing anything. What they are doing is taking a broad general objective and then turning it into specific plans and activities that can be militarily accomplished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One clarification with the number of this document is necessary. There was quite a lot of confusion which I created as well. The number of Directive 7 is P1214. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is correct. And Directive 7(1) is P1199.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question has to do with Directive 7(1). We were reading item 5.3, the decisions. Were you able to see there if the Main Staff detailed, in any of the items of 7(1), the attack on Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have P1199 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have P1199, page 5, paragraph 5.3, which contains the decision for the Drina Corps because it is within its area of responsibility that Srebrenica and Zepa lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there mention of Srebrenica and Zepa anywhere here? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 5.3, there is no specific mention of Srebrenica or Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, can these directives be the basis for Operation Krivaja and Stupcanica which are not mentioned in any of the decisions of the Supreme Commander or the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure they can, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just if the general could give a slow description of the other operation so the court reporter can get it down directly. We clearly see Krivaja which we all know but the other one is a little harder to say, but I think its important to say to catch it here in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you repeat the names of these operations. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tolimir mentioned Operations Krivaja and Stupcanica, S-t-u-p-c-a-n-i-c-a.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Krivaja is the operation in the direction of Srebrenica and Stupcanica in the direction of Zepa. Are they at all mentioned in the directive? That was my question to Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief did you not say that they were the basis for the activities in Srebrenica and Zepa? Do you recall that or do you want me to give you the references? Did you not speak of them as a basis for the activities taken in respect of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to the first part of your question, yes, I do recall saying that 7 and 7(1) were the basis of the activities in Srebrenica and Zepa. And I also believe, yes, Directive 7 specifically lays out the framework for the basis of activities taken with respect to the civilian population. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your testimony will be the basis on which the Trial Chamber will take its decision. Can you refer precisely to the portions of Directive 7(1) which the Main Staff sent to its subordinate units which speak to the attitude to be taken toward the civilian population, or, better said, where exactly does Directive 7(1) deal with this issue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said before, Directive 7(1) does not specifically deal with those issues, at least in the sense of laying them out in a military sense or military terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We have completed the analysis of Directives 7 and 7(1). This is my question: The units which receive these directives, do they use them to extract their own tasks or assignments on this basis? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they do. Their -- they can either extract them directly or in cases, based on these documents, the Main Staff itself may issue further orders directing the corps to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you list any element of Directive 7(1) which would serve as the basis for further activities intended to create unbearable conditions? Can you list at least one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If possible, before I answer a document based on the entire -- you know, a question on the entire document, I would like to see the entire document just to quickly refresh my memory on it. It is a somewhat lengthy document, and before I just give a quick yes-or-no answer I would like to just scan through the it for a minute or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Since we are pressed for time, we will give you an opportunity to answer the question after the break during which you would be able to consult the text, if Their Honours are in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I would be satisfied with that. I do think it's important that he be allowed to do that, and I think that that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document should be given to the witness when we break. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, during your direct examination you were asked what the role of the assistant commander for intelligence would be in implementing the directives, and your answer was in relation to security, specifically; that's page 16483, lines 1 to 9, of the transcript of the 12th of July 2011.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 12th of July, 1995, 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I'm quoting: "From the point of view of security, one needs to make sure of what the actual plan and intention of the VRS is and to make sure that it remains concealed from the UN and the international community, and this requires for its security and counter-intelligence sector to make assure that there is no leakage of information which is key to that plan. Therefore, it needs to be privy to the details of the plan in order to ensure that the intelligence and security sector may carry out all the missions required to be achieved in order to support these objectives." I am asking you this as a military expert: Is it the security organs that are charged with protecting the confidentiality and secrecy of information or is it within the purview of the commander of the units carrying out these operations? Under whose charge are all the personnel involved? Is this the role of the security organs or is their role to exercise control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the concept of the VRS, the commander's always responsible. However, particularly with technical issues like security, the commander heavily relies on and uses his trained security officers to implement these security measures. So again while the commander is always responsible, security falls well within -- and the protection of information and counter-intelligence, those types of things, fall well within the security technical chain and while all individuals have a role in it, the predominant role is going to be played by those individuals who are members of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, should intelligence and security organs be aware of all the details of a military operation in order to do counter-intelligence work which constitutes 80 per cent of their duties? This is something that you stated during your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe they do. I base my belief on the doctrinal writings of the JNA, and as they were applied by the VRS, which gives the assistant commander of intelligence and security at the various levels, it puts him as part of the commander's primary staff. That gives him that ability to keep fully apprised of what is going on. Again, going back to the practical aspect of both collecting information as well as counter-intelligence, it's vital for the person who is protecting the information or seeking to collect information to support the plan to know what the plan is. Without that basic knowledge, these individuals would not know how to structure or organise their activities to support the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if security organs propose measures to commanders, who ultimately carries out these measures, these same security organs or the commanders of their units? Let's say if one of the measures is confidentiality and protection of confidential data.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, using that particular issue and keeping in mind that there are some security tasks that the security branch doesn't have to co-ordinate with the commander, a task like this would be proposed to the commander, the measures that they would take to secure the confidentiality and protection of data, for example, classified documents, it would certainly be customary for the security officer to propose a plan for the commander, to have the commander's authorisation of that plan, and it to be implemented in that manner. It would not be a situation, normally, where the security officer in and of itself implement a plan effecting the remainder of the command and not do so without having the approval of the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question: Who is the one who carries out the measures proposed by the security organ, the security organ himself or the commander and his subordinates? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it depends on the task. In this particular scenario that you have laid out, the security organ would propose the procedures to be implemented, the commander would approve them, and they would be carried out by the individuals who actually had to deal with the documents to make sure that they were secured, keeping in mind that it will be more than security officers, other officers will be involved. The security officer's role then becomes to ensure that the plan, as it has been written, is being followed by those other officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this is the appropriate time for our first break. The Chamber is grateful, Mr. Butler, if you would look through the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Don't forget it here in the courtroom. We adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we continue with the examination, I would like to raise one matter. This morning we received a response of the Defence in relation to the subpoena motion for Witness X. We would like to -- I would like to ask you, Mr. McCloskey, at the end of today's hearing, if you have additional information in relation to that witness, if the Prosecution was able to contact the witness, for instance, through VWS or another way. But perhaps the OTP is able to prepare some additional information if there is some available at the end of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you've looked at these documents. Could you now provide an answer, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The document again that we are referring to is P1199, and I would draw your attention to the English language translation page 4. In context it is found in paragraph 4 where it relates to the strategic decisions of the commander of the VRS discussing his general goals and how they will be carried out, and in this particular passage - which is the second paragraph from the top of page 4 in the English language translation - it states as follows: "Other forces of the VRS shall contribute to the conduct of Operation Sadjestvo 95 with the goal of operative strategic camouflage and correcting the operative tactical position by carrying out planned combat battle and operations in accordance with Directive number 7 and active combat operations toward Bugojno, Travnik, Kladanj, Olovo, and Vares and around the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde enclaves and the Bihac Pocket." So in this context, General Mladic is raising as part of his general strategy that he anticipates that there will be offensive combat operations to some degree directed against the enclaves. Now, finally, to circle it back around with the issue of Krivaja 95 and its association with Directive 7 and 7(1), I would remind the Court that in the documents that the Drina Corps produced where they laid out the plan Krivaja 95, they specifically referenced in this operations plan that this plan was in response to or in furtherance of the guidance that it received under Directive 7 and 7(1). So in light of the fact that the corps staff and the corps plan that are planning and implementing Krivaja 95 they believe that that plan is in furtherance of Directive 7 and 7(1). I am just not sure how it can be divorced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you help me with one explanation. You are referring to Krivaja 95. In this paragraph you have read into the transcript, there is a reference to Operation Sadjestvo 95. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I don't believe that this operation as envisioned has to do specifically with Krivaja 95. I believe this is a larger operation that has to do with another area, particularly around the Posavina corridor or other areas. I don't believe that -- essentially what this paragraph is saying that while Sadjestvo 95 is the major operation, other corps units are going to be involved in other actions that will have some general supporting function, even if it's simply by attacking in other areas keeping the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Croatian forces from being able to reinforce what their main attack is. So it's not directly connected, but just like everywhere else within VRS, when you attack in one area of the country, you are creating the circumstances where your enemy has to defend and is not available then to be transferred to where you believe your main objective is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I have just heard you when you were reading saying around Zepa and Srebrenica. It reads "around Zepa and Srebrenica," not "in Zepa and Srebrenica." Am I right or did you read something different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The English language translation that I have specifies -- the language that it uses is: Combat operations towards three various locations and "around the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde enclaves and the Bihac Pocket."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thus it is "around the enclaves," not "in the enclaves." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I don't believe that in this document that they envision actually violating the safe area. Their object is combat in and around -- or, I'm sorry, to be clear, on the perimeter and around the safe area. This is not a call to actually attack the towns of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You've also said in this context: Is General Tolimir supposed to know about what lower commands are writing or should lower commands derive their orders from higher level directives? Is the Main Staff supposed to know what brigades and other lower level units are ordering their men, or is it the other way around, should brigades and subordinate commands be guided by what the Main Staff is ordering?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of your question, sure, the -- it is the Main Staff which provides the broader guidance down to the subordinate levels, in this case the corps and two brigades. The other side of the coin is, yes, absolutely, it's the Main Staff's responsibility to know and to monitor whether or not those plans are being implemented properly. For example, using the command and staff processes that were in place at the time, when a corps develops a large plan, the Main Staff is going to be aware of the details of this plan. It's customary within the context of the VRS when putting together plans that, at the level that the brigade or the level of whatever it was planned, that the next higher formation, you know, would be briefed on what the commander's plan was, how he proposed to carry it out, so the higher level command would have an awareness of what was going on, why it was happening, and to ensure that it was in compliance with the broader strategy. So, I mean, specifically I can't envision is a situation where the Drina Corps command and staff would have created the operations plan for Krivaja 95 and that the Main Staff would have had no awareness of that plan. It would have had to have been brought to the attention of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you kindly look at 16330, lines 12 through 15, dated 8 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where you say in response to Mr. McCloskey's question: "Does Tolimir's assignment have to do with the protection of the plan of operations? Is it a kind of military secret?" He said. And you replied: "Yes, absolutely," and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the witness please wait for the transcript. Now we have the relevant portion on the screen. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said "yes." Now, I should like to ask you, in the documents that you spoke about, is crime treated as a military secret and should a plan on crimes be protected by the security organ although it is forbidden by international conventions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. The quote that you read me is so short that I don't recall exactly what context we were discussing when I gave the answer. Is it possible to read a larger passage of that transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry that we didn't provide you with it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the transcript before you. Reference 16331, lines 12 through 15. Sorry, reference 16330, lines 12 through 15. Now, I am asking you if General Tolimir is protecting these plans --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could I ask you to just wait until I've finished reading it and then please ask your question, if I may? Thank you. Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Is crime a military secret and should security organs be involved in the protection of such a military secret if it is forbidden, prohibited by international conventions as a crime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of crime, I assume you're referring to issues like war crimes and things of that nature, correct? Not strictly domestic or other forms of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is war crime a military secret?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many jurisdictions, military jurisdictions, the fact that military forces may have comitted war crimes would be considered to be confidential. It would not be an issue that would often want to be disclosed. Legally, there are obligations under international law, but practically speaking, for those individuals who were seeking to evade responsibility, one of the methods that they would use to evade responsibility would be to make any information about the conduct of those crimes secrets, so they would have the official powers of the state to classify those types of secrets as a way to cloud the details of the acts that occurred. So there is a legal answer and then there is the practical reality of the scope of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if you say a war crime is not a secret but would be considered confidential, could it be contrary to the legislation of the country concerned and the legislation of the international community stipulating that crimes must be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Those countries obviously, and most states for that matter, have laws that will require them to investigate and prosecute those responsible for war crimes. Having said that, the practical reality is that the public disclosure of war crimes that have been comitted by forces of a particular state can have a particularly damaging impact on a nation's war effort. One, which is why they are to be avoided but also why that knowledge of them tends to be restricted to very limited circles because of their immediate impact on war objectives. I think if one goes back and brings this back into the context of what we are talking about, if one looks at the document that were drafted by the VRS itself in 1992 where they discussed the measures -- in part of that document where they discuss the measures relating to the prevention of war crimes by the VRS, they very candidly acknowledged what the impact of being involved in those crimes could be to the struggle of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if something is secret to the perpetrator, is it also secret for the state and the organs who are bound to act in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly envision that if the perpetrator were the state that it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am talking about an individual. Would security organs and services in the army be duty-bound to prosecute perpetrators of offences and crimes or would they be inclined to protect them as you claimed a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of the VRS, as laid out, security organs as part of their crime prevention and investigation responsibilities, are duty-bound to investigate allegations of war crimes against an individual. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I would appreciate it in order to save time if you could give brief answers whenever possible so that we avoid repeating explanations that have already been given. My question is: Since you refer to crimes in documents from 1992, have you seen documents from July 1995 that speak about the prohibition of perpetrating crimes? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of documents that raise that issue. I mean, I think the one you are referring to might possibly be the order by President Karadzic on 10 July 1995 where he directs that the military forces moving into Srebrenica operate in conjunction of the Geneva Conventions. Is that the document you're referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We finally got an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at D41. It's a document from the Main Staff of the VRS, dated 9 July. Sent to the president of Republika Srpska for his information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you can see I am not lying, he ordered it, to the forward command post of the Drina Corps, Generals Gvero and Krstic personally. Conduct of combat operation, and it says: "In keeping with the order of the President of Republika Srpska, issue an order to all combat units involved in combat operations around Srebrenica to provide maximum protection to UNPROFOR members and the Muslim civilian population. Order your subordinate units to refrain from devastating civilian targets unless they are forced to as a result of strong resistance from the enemy. Prohibit the torching of residential buildings, and treat the civilian population and prisoners of war in keeping with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949. "Signed, Major General Zdravko Tolimir." Is it the case then that units involved in operations around Srebrenica received this order in good time that was sent to them through their superior commands as early as 9 July? Does the stamp show that they have received it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to the units, but certainly with respect to the individuals named who it was sent to, Generals Gvero and Krstic at the Drina Corps IKM, the stamp reflects that they would have received this order in the time that you specify. I mean, certainly before the operation would have gone down on 10 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since they received it, were they required to forward it to their subordinate units, this order from the Supreme Commander, as all other instructions for further combat operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last paragraph of the document, the first page, it specifies that "in accordance with the order ... you must issue an order to combat units ..." So an order had to be issued. Whether it was nearly are a retransmission of this order, as we have seen in other documents signed by General Krstic or as the Drina Corps -- or the commander of the IKM or whether he chose to draft his own order reflecting these principles, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Can you answer this question: General Tolimir, as a signatory of this document, did he not openly write about war crimes and propose public measures aimed at preventing those from happening at the same time as these measures are carried out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in this particular document you did lay out in paragraph 3 the expectations of the President of the Republika Srpska, and in paragraph 4, again, it appears that you are amplifying the expectations or the directions of the President of the Republika Srpska, and you lay out specific concrete issues relating to actions that have to be taken so that crimes are avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are security organs here referring to what the lawful conduct in these units should be? Aren't they publically pointing their finger to these issues, or are they concealing and suppressing these facts in the documents sent out to the various units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I take your question correctly, what you are doing is relaying the instructions of the president of the Republika Srpska to the subordinate individuals, in this case General Gvero and General Krstic - more General Krstic since he's the actual commander of the operation at this time - and you're laying it out in clear terms. It is not being handled as a document, and this material is not being kept from him or anyone else. And, in fact, as you noted, the fact that the president of the Republika Srpska has directed that supplemental orders be issued reflects the fact that there was a desire on the part of the president of the Republika Srpska to ensure that not only did the Drina Corps command have this but their subordinate formations understood what the expectations were upon them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If up and down the chain of command and information there is a flow of information about the respect for the Geneva Conventions and the ban on the commission of war crimes, are in that case the security organs under an obligation to comply with these instructions and are not the perpetrators of such crimes going to try to conceal their crimes from Tolimir and others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of July 1995, I am not sure how impart -- the security branch -- you know, the security branch's interest in concealing the crimes is a direct result of their involvement in them. So I am not sure -- I mean, in an abstract theory where non-security organs are seeking to investigate a crime that have been comitted by others, I agree that those people perpetrating the acts are going to seek to keep them secret from the security branch. However, as the evidence is laid out with respect of these events, the security branch was complicit in the actual conduct of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And such organs, if they were perpetrators, did they not conceal their crimes also from those who issue orders that crimes be prosecuted and who ask that measures be taken to prevent the commission of crimes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in abstract, perpetrators of those crimes would seek to do that. Again, with July 1995 as the context, given the widespread scope of the crimes and the thousands of people that were killed in such short days, I believe that the evidence that is out there has made it clear that the widespread knowledge of the crimes was so large because so many people were involved that to a large degree it was impossible for that information not to believe to be available to anybody who chose to look for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you know that an OTP witness and a convict for the war crimes, Momir Nikolic, said in -- during this trial that he was not aware of the contents of the information dated the 9th, which refers to the Geneva Conventions and the prohibition of war crimes, and are you aware of him stating this in front of this Trial Chamber? I am asking you this because his testimony was given in open court.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not follow his testimony, so I am not aware of what Momir Nikolic may or may not have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will show his testimony to you now. Or let me first show you the document that he personally received.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D64 displayed, thank you. This is D64.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It speaks about the registration of the prisoners of war which is a proper measure to prevent any abuse. Is not the registration of prisoners of war one of the first steps in a series of measures to ensure that crimes are not comitted against POWs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the section that the general is referring to is on the next page in the English, so it would -- I am not sure where it's on the B/C/S, but it may be helpful for all parties for us to see that section he's speaking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could it be enlarged a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The last paragraph that the OTP wanted to see reads: "In view of the importance to arrest as many of the dispersed Muslim units as possible, it is also necessary to register all the able-bodied men in the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. "The organs for security affairs will inform the MUP units in their areas of responsibility of their tasks and co-ordinate their activities with them." Is not the involvement of the MUP in this issue, as well as all the other measures taken, including the registration of the POWs, one of the first steps taken with a view to ensuring that the public character of the activities surrounding the POWs rather than secrecy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I note that the interpretation we have received was not exactly the same as the translation of the document in front of us. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I know the translators do their best, but I think the problem is if the general could, especially on such important paragraphs, point out to the translation -- well, to all of us what paragraphs he's talking about, because they weren't obviously able to catch -- otherwise they would have read it. And I -- and this is important because the official version says "make lists of," it doesn't say "register." And I don't know if that's a translation or what that is, but if we could try to make sure that something like this that the translators have a chance, otherwise we are getting these conflicting versions of an important document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The relevant part is in paragraph 3, and especially that one that Mr. McCloskey is referring to is the following, I quote: "It is equally importantly to note down the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari." Mr. Butler, are you able to answer the question which is still on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question just went off the top of my scene, sir. If I could ask for a little assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was, I read it to you: "Is not --" Perhaps the transcript is not correct. It's related to the involvement of the MUP in this issue and as well as other matters taken, including the registration of POWs, is one of the first steps taken with a view to ensuring that the public character of the activities surrounding the POWs rather than secrecy. That was more or less the question. Can you provide us with an answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure whether it's an issue of public character versus secrecy. The requirement to register prisoners of war has to do with accountability. I guess perhaps getting closer to General Tolimir's intention, prisoners who are not registered technically do not exist, and as a result, without registering them and without an acknowledgment that they are in the custody of a warring party, there is no provision or there is no way that the protections offered by the Geneva Conventions through the offices of the ICRC or any other body can be enforced. So in that context I think that's the right answer. I mean, it's for accountability because, once they are accountable, the warring party incurs a responsibility for their treatment and for their safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this a reference to the lists that are to be drawn of all those who are being evacuated or all those who are to become prisoners of war but who do not surrender?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In this particular document what is being laid out is that if one looks at the context of the prior paragraph, it specifically says that the Muslims wish to portray Srebrenica as a demilitarised zone with nothing but a civilian population. As a consequence, the following paragraph said, therefore, it's equally important to note down the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UN base at Potocari.
