So for the first component, it's a very strict definition of whose names need to be -- or which group of individual men have to be listed. And, to your second point, while I agree that listing those names would raise the issue of their accountability as potential prisoners of war, I take it from this document that the primary purpose of those lists was to be able to come back at such future point in time and make the case on behalf of the VRS that the people who were in Potocari and in this Srebrenica demilitarised zone were, in fact, military members as well as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. The document is there for the Trial Chamber to decide on rather than me or you. I have no more time to spend on this. This is my question: Did not General Tolimir clearly express his view here that as many Muslim formations -- formations that do not mount any resistance should be arrested, and those that do, that they should be liquidated, and that a record should be made also of those that are being evacuated from the base in Potocari? And if they are arrested, that doesn't mean that they would be killed -- at least that was not my order that they should be arrested and killed; is that right? Or is this something that slipped your mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your last part of your question first, I agree this order does not specifically have an order from General Tolimir to kill prisoners. Again, it also talks about -- the second part of it discusses the importance to arrest or, I take it, capture as many members of these units as possible. The third part, of course, is, when we are talking about listing the names down, again - and it may be the way that the document is translated, I hold that open, obviously - but you are specifically noting in this document that the lists are those individuals who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. There is not a specific reference in the document that all men captured will be listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Do you see the memo where it says the command of the 2nd Brigade, and it says Motorised Brigade, strictly confidential, 13th of July, 1995. Does it not indicate that the units received it on the 13th of July, 1995? At least that's what the stamp testifies to.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that the stamp, as you've mentioned, indicates that this particular document was received by that particular unit, on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show page 1 for the witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see that it says in the addressees -- among the addressees are the Pribicevac IKM and the Bratunac IKM, and all the intelligence and security organs which are then listed below. Does it not mean that the document was delivered to all the subordinate intelligence and security organs of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, East Bosnian Corps, and the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The way that I take this, the document -- if you look at the second line of the addressee list, "to the command of the SRK and IBK," it's to their corps commands. So from your question I don't agree that it was delivered to all the subordinate intelligence and security organs of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and East Bosnia Corps. I would -- then further down it lists the specific intelligence organs within the framework of the Drina Corps as well as the state security apparatus which received this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, let me read this so that we can save time. I will read it out and then you can say whether what I read out is correct or not. Is not the telegram sent to: "The intelligence and security departments of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, East Bosnia Corps, the Pribicevac IKM, and Bratunac IKM, and the intelligence and security organs of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade," that was Nikolic's, "the Milici Brigade, Zvornik Brigade, the Romanija Podrinje, Rogatica, and the RDB of MUP including the MUP of the RS." Is that not stated among the addressees ahead of the body of text? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But again I would remind you that that was not your original question. Your original question was whether or not the document was delivered to all the subordinate intelligence and security organs of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, East Bosnia Corps, and Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record. I followed your reading, Mr. Tolimir. I found most of the units you were referring to, but not the Rogatica brigade. I don't find it in this list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's stated as the "1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, but in addition you were referring Rogatica Brigade. I don't find it in the list. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is its document. And the stamp says: "The command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade." And somebody probably omitted the Rogatica Brigade. I suppose that the person who drafted it omitted the Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But this is my question for Mr. Butler: The extent of addressees to which the document was sent, does it not guarantee to the person who drafts the document that as many units as possible will receive the document and carry out the assignments contained within?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- what it guarantees is that the person who drafted the document and created the addressee list is that it is that person's intention that those formations or those units receive this order. So if you list down who the addressees are on this particular document, it is your intent that the communications centre send it to those subscribers. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this a way to suppress or conceal activities and measures or is the purpose of the document to make them public since they are described in written documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be clear, we are not talking about public or concealed. The reality is this document is a strictly confidential military document. It is not public. But within the context of the military, what this document is and what the author is doing is ensuring that all of the units who he believed had a relevant role in the process were as fully informed as what were going on as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said "public or concealed." Is strictly confidential not a designation available to all the documents available to personnel and addressees -- or, rather, does it not mean that it is available to personnel and the addressees and should remain concealed from those outside of the army and is this not standard practice in the armies world-wide? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And I think it's a terminology issue between what I would view public and maybe perhaps what you view as public. Those individuals within the military who were appropriately cleared, as most officers would be, this document is a document that they are designed to see, if it is addressed to them. So in that sense it is not a protected document that it's going to be concealed from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can this document be concealed from the prosecutors and investigators in the army who work on the detection and prosecution of crimes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If those individuals were appropriately cleared, and the appropriate authority designated that they were to be given this document as part of a war crimes investigation, it would be given to them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, did you see this document when you were reviewing other documentation? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the transcript of 7 April, page 12531, to see what Nikolic said in lines 13 and 14. 12513 is the number of the page. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. If you have had a look at his statement, could you tell us whether it is the case that even before this Court he said he had not received that document and he could have received it in two ways. First of all, his brigade is among the addressees; and second, he was at the forward command post of Bratunac where Popovic was also with him because Popovic was one of the addressees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think in the first part of your question it was a misrepresentation of what we can see in the transcript. Literally, Mr. Nikolic says, I quote: "I cannot state with full certainty, but I think I have not seen this document before, although I see that my brigade is one of the intended recipients. But I cannot state with any certainty that it arrived or did not arrive." This is different from what you said. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was speaking based on my own notes, but if you are reading the transcript then you must be right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Should Mr. Nikolic have been aware of this document, in your opinion, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is addressed to the security organ of the Bratunac Brigade, he was the assistant commander for intelligence and security. Assuming that it arrived there and that there weren't any communication difficulties, and I take it that it probably did arrive, communications were relatively good. It should have been brought to his attention, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Is Mr. Nikolic answerable to his commander who also received the telegram and his own security organ, or is he answerable to someone outside that command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As discussed within the various regulations, I mean, he's always answerable to his immediate commander at the brigade, which was Colonel Blagojevic, but for a strict line of technical supervision he would have been answerable to Colonel Popovic, who was his superior within the Drina Corps security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Could General Tolimir assign his powers to others and vice versa in keeping with rules of engagement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general principle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphones should be switched off while you are discussing with your assistant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a general principle of command, you are entitled to delegate various authorities to subordinates in order for them to accomplish missions. Again, as part of that, the fact that you delegate certain authorities to subordinates still leaves you responsible for the overall success or failure of the subordinates to accomplish those tasks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D202. It's the rule on the powers of a corps of land forces in peacetime. We see the first page in both versions. It's the book of rules on the powers of a corps command of land forces in peacetime. We need page 4, paragraph 4 -- in fact, Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "The organs of the command may not assign their powers to other command organs or transfer their responsibility to the organs of a lower command unless specifically authorised to do so." My question is in view of this stipulation, could General Tolimir be held responsible for what was within the purview of lower-ranking units, corps, and brigades, and were they able to transfer to him affairs that were within their area of responsibility which would make him answerable for what they were supposed to be responsible for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that this particular article refers to the proposition that you laid out. This particular article lays out the proposition that a commander cannot unilaterally transfer the scope of responsibility -- or command organs to other command organs take on tasks of the appropriate organ or of a different command until specifically authorised to do so. I don't take that in the same manner as the issue that we've discussed before, which is your ability to delegate the authority to your subordinates to implement orders and your responsibility to ensure that those subordinates have carried out the orders, or to take measures that they have not. I think this is a completely different issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at the transcript of the 8th, page 16340, lines 24, 25, and see what you said there. And then I can ask my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you've read it, let us know. Thank you. Can you tell us what you meant by this when you said he orders security organs and General Tolimir receives authorisations? Who do I get them from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have I had -- do I have the right part highlighted? I don't understand the question in context of the transcript. Okay. Let me go further down. I'm sorry. Okay. I think I know what you are getting at now. Could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am saying did you say here, when you're saying, "he's not ordering in this document," are you saying that the commander is not giving orders to security organs but that it is General Tolimir who issues orders to them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the document that we were discussing, this document had to do with the various interrelationships between the corps, the Main Staff, and the security organs and the security organs' roles and responsibilities. And as part of the discussion, it was related to which authority -- under what circumstances it would be the commander who issues orders to the security organs for those tasks that are under the commander's purview, and then the commander -- in this case the commander of the Drina Corps, I believe, yes, was saying back that for those specific tasks that are directly related to your counter-intelligence and security function, those particular tasks will be regulated back through the security chain, ultimately General Tolimir. So the context of the document and the discussion is to the security organs so they understand that the Drina Corps, so they understand who regulates which specific tasks and under what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Tell us, please, was General Tolimir able to issue orders to the organs of the Drina Corps or can he only -- could he only give them guidance in their work? Could he only professionally train them to carry out that order of the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that question entirely depends upon the specificity of the task. And again, for the examples that were laid out, I believe question discussed one particular example where the task at hand was strictly a counter-intelligence task related to a potential security threat to various senior officers of the VRS. And when one looks at the orders that were issued there, it's clear that they were coming directly from the Main Staff and through the security chain to the various subordinates. In that case, General Tolimir is issuing direct orders to those security officers because it falls within the confines of that narrow and already designated responsibility. In the essence, for example, where the security organ is discussing issues related to the use of the military police, it would be far more appropriate for General Tolimir and the Main Staff to publish, through the security channels, guidance and recommendations to the corps commanders as to how the military police should be organised and how they should be trained. But ultimately because that task belongs to the command side and does not fall on the strictly technical side, again, the best that you would be able to do is to advise and recommend. It ultimately would be the corps commander who was responsible for the military police, his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If he's responsible, does he then also issue orders whereas I only provide guidance? Isn't it the case that security organs only provide guidance to his subordinates? Is he the one who issues orders based on those proposals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we be more specific? He said "to his subordinates," but I believe we have been talking about a corps commander. So Mr. Butler doesn't have to guess what subordinates we are talking about and so the answer makes sense, could we ask for more specificity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you make your question more precise, then you will be able to receive a very precise answer, I suppose. Perhaps you can rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in any situation whatsoever, could General Tolimir issue orders to the subordinate units of the Drina Corps or was he only able to give them professional guidance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to actual units, you were not authorised to give orders to those subordinate units. You're only authorised within the purview of the intelligence and security organ to directly give orders to individuals who are members of the intelligence and security branch within the confines of their specific counter-intelligence and other security functions. So there is not a situation where I envision where General Tolimir could call down, for example, and give direct orders to the commander of the Drina Corps Military Police Battalion. Those would have to go through the corps based on General Tolimir's recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You said during examination-in-chief something about plans for killing. Do you recall that? If you recall that, could you tell us whether a plan for the killing of Muslims existed at all, and if so, have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my examination-in-chief, I discussed a great deal about plans for killing. If I take your question, was there actually a written order laying out a plan, if there was I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you heard evidence that a plan existed and that certain individuals were involved in it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As -- not withstanding what evidence I have heard, as a result of my research and as a result of the various documents that I've assembled as part of that research, I believe that those show clear evidence that a plan did exist, the plan was implemented, and there were various numbers of individuals who took actions, in part, in support of this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You believe it, but could you present to the Court any reference, any evidence showing that a plan, a verbal or written one, existed, and can you tell us who were the participants in that plan? Who made it? When? Where? When was that meeting held, because a plan has to be discussed and accepted somewhere at some time, at some place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary presentation that I would offer the Court with respect to that is the Srebrenica revised military narrative that I have offered where I lay that document out as the foundation of what I believe are the circumstances and the inherent plan that led to those circumstances. I have also laid out in the course of my testimony here and discussed a broad variety of documents that were not available to me at the time when I drafted the military revised narrative, and I've testified to how I believe those documents that were not available to me at the time further support the conclusions that I made in my previous narrative. So that's the short answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. To provide a clear and concise answer to that would take days on Mr. Butler's part, literally. I think he gave us an outline, but of course that's possible, but in this context it's really not -- it was never what he was called for about to make those conclusions based on the evidence that you're hearing. So I just want to -- he, of course, can answer that in detail if the Court wishes, but I am not sure it's really appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler has spent a lot of days with us here in the courtroom, and Mr. Tolimir asked the witness to provide him with short answers. He did. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On transcript page 16326 of the 8th, lines 18 through 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you this. He said: "I suppose Tolimir was aware that Muslim men were being separated from women with certain intentions," et cetera, et cetera. And you replied, on page 16363, lines 1 through 10: "That proves that at that time that General Tolimir did not know of that plan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we don't have the right part on the screen. Please check again the page and wait for the -- that this will appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 16326, lines 18 through 15, Mr. McCloskey asked the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Now we have it on the screen. Thank you. It's really a different page than the first one you have mentioned. Now please continue. It can't be lines 18 through 15. Perhaps through 15 of the next page. Please be precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my notes I noted that it was in lines 18 through 15. Page 16362, lines 18 through 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Lines 18 through 15 is reading back. Perhaps you mean 15 through 18.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry. Well noted, but it actually begins at 18 and goes on until line 25. I noted it down wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps let Mr. Butler have the opportunity to read that part and then put your question. Mr. Tolimir, your question, please. The last one before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you said in your answer: "The plan had not yet reached Tolimir." Does it mean that Tolimir was completely unaware of the plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am not sure that, Mr. Tolimir, is informed in this way in this part of the transcript. I have to correct myself. I wanted to say, please, tell us where exactly you find that part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From line 18 on page 16362 until line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In these lines there is no mention of Mr. Tolimir. I would suggest that you check that with your assistant and we break now and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue, but please bear in mind that we have to stop some minutes earlier than usual to enable us to discuss some procedural matters. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, to shorten the time necessary in view of what Their Honours said, can we now show 16360, that's the page of the transcript of the 8th, up until 136 -- up until 16361, ending up with line 17 on page 16361.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the starting line from the previous page of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the starting line on page 16360. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The line is 22 and the court officer has marked it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Butler, in the section as marked here, did you not state that Tolimir had not been aware of the plan at the time because it had not reached him at that point? Otherwise, you say he would not have been reporting to, et cetera, et cetera, had he been privy to the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is clearly in relation to a document which talks about the time and place that this answer has to do with. So if we could have that document it will make it much more clear so the answer will make more sense to everyone, because we were dealing with that document at the time and I don't think that there is any contest about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is document D64 and we'll display it. The date is the 7th of April, 2011. D64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you misspoke. It can't be the year 2011. It's the 12th of July, 1995, this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, would General Tolimir have been writing this document had he been familiar with the plan you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As noted in the transcript, the Prosecution had raised the proposition that if a plan had been made in the early hours of 12 July to kill the people that were being assembled or kill everybody, and that later on 12 July, if General Tolimir drafted this document reflecting his expectation that lists should be made of the people in Potocari, does it indicate that he had been told at that point in time that an order had already been given that there would no lists because the individuals were going to be killed, my answer was that this document does not indicate that General Tolimir at that time would have been aware that the plan was -- that the people who were being separated in Potocari, the military-aged men would ultimately be killed. As I said in my original answer, I don't believe that if General Tolimir was aware that that was the plan as directed by General Mladic at the time, that he would have placed the guidance that he did with respect to registering -- or making a list of the military-aged men in Potocari in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, please look at page 2 of the document in order to see at what particular time this document was handed over to be coded and sent out to units. We can see that in the lower right-hand corner of the original. Where it is stated the 12th of July, 1995, at 2150. Does this mean that nothing could have been known of this so-called plan of which you say was made in the morning of the 12th at the time when I was in Rogatica at 2150 of the 12th when this document was made? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could the Court please go back to the first page of this document in English and scroll to the top? To answer the second part of your question first, I believe I have testified on this document that by virtue of it having a number of the Drina Corps command 17/897, that when you drafted this document you were at the headquarters of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, not Rogatica. So I don't agree with your assertion that at that time that this document was done, it was -- that you were not in Vlasenica. I believe that's exactly where you were. I don't know at what point in time after you drafted this document -- okay. I don't know at what time after you drafted this document which contains information up to 1945 hours in the body of it. So it kind of puts a timestamp on the internals of the document between that time and then when you may have left afterwards for Rogatica, but when this document was physically drafted by you and written for the communication centre, you were in Vlasenica. So now getting back to the first part of your question, again using the prospect that the Prosecution has laid out about when a plan was to kill the individuals who were being separated at Potocari, the men, I again go back to the fact that I don't believe that you would have written the guidance related to making lists of those military-aged men if you were aware that General Mladic already made a decision that they were to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, so this document was made on the 12th and reached the units only on the 13th. Did you know about a document according to which on the 13th Mladic had brought over the journalists to film the prisoners of war? Would Mladic have done so, would he have brought the journalists over to film the scene had he made the plan and did he make the plan at all to begin with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a compound problem. You should split it up into different questions. It is easier to answer. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and if he could refer to what he -- where in the record we have a film that Mladic has filmed prisoners of war in Potocari or what, in more in particular, he means by that because it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir doesn't say that Mladic filmed prisoners of war but that he brought over journalists to film prisoners of war. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, I apologise for my inartful way, but what is he specifically referring to, if he could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please try to rephrase your question so that it is easier for the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The Main Staff and General Mladic taken the decision on the 12th, as the Prosecutor claims, would Mladic have asked that journalists be allowed access to the area on the 13th to film them and take statements from them, and would Mladic himself have decided to appear on that very location himself, as he did? This was stated by Mr. Zoran Malic [as interpreted] as OTP witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We got Zoran Malic. Does the General mean Zoran Malinic? Because that will have some meaning for the witness, perhaps. I see Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, errors happen in the transcript, especially when it comes to name. It is Mr. Malinic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am unaware of the testimony of Mr. Zoran Malinic in this case, so I cannot comment as to what he did or did not say. And I certainly cannot comment with respect to what General Mladic was or was not thinking with respect to journalists. I can say that, as the Court is aware and has been discussed, there were various orders that were going out from the Main Staff with respect to controlling access to ensure that prisoners weren't being exposed and journalists weren't being permitted to come in unless they had authority. And I guess as a practical aspect General Mladic, in order the get what he wanted, was willing to assume the risk, that those cameras may have picked up parts of what was going on that were not intended to be seen by General Mladic, which is, in fact, exactly what happened in the Petrovic video which took place on 13 July, 1995. So I am not aware of the details that you are talking about with respect to Mr. Malinic or why General Mladic may or may not have made decisions as to video cameras and what his intent was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at Exhibit D289. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have Mr. Malinic's statement there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 18. Or, actually, page 17 in English and 16 in Serbian. The last paragraph in English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote Zoran Malinic: "I don't know why it had to be issued. I told you I received an order that the TV crews can come. And I think these TV crews came through the press-centre of the Main Staff that was located in Han Pijesak. And I think they did come and videotaped. It is possible that they were forbidden to videotape since it was combat activities taking place. Especially if we are talking about foreign TV crews that could be the source of intelligence for the enemies. I think the individual who decided that filming should be allowed said I don't know what, but I think he approved it. I think it's the Main Staff who approved it. I think the commander of the protection regiment could not have decided to allow these TV crews to come and videotape." Mr. Butler, this statement by Mr. Malinic, D289, which was taken on the 2nd of December, 2005, does it not clearly indicate that TV crews were present at the stadium in Kasaba and that they were filming? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were or not. I am aware that Colonel Milutin Milutinovic - I believe I have his name correctly - who was the head of the VRS media center was in Srebrenica as a member of the Main Staff and that there was at least one camera crew from the Main Staff's press-information centre taking various footage. I don't recall that I've ever actually seen that, and I am not sure whether or not the Office of the Prosecutor has ever interviewed Colonel Milutinovic. If they did, it's not an interview I am aware of. So again, Colonel Malinic has his view of what he saw or did not see. I mean, I am aware generally that there was some military media there, as well as Zoran Petrovic, but I don't know that I can comment any further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. The context of the question needs to be made more clear. What particular area is General Tolimir talking about, because it's clear where Zoran Malinic is and where he is talking about in his answers, but that part was not shown to him. So I think the general will get a better answer from Mr. Butler if he at least tells Mr. Butler the area that we're talking about, the geographic area that we are talking about, or that Zoran Malinic is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you know that Colonel Malinic was in Nova Kasaba and that that was the point of crossing for the Muslims making their way from Srebrenica towards Kladanj and that they surrendered and that as prisoners they were located in Nova Kasaba. What is your knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree. Then Major Zoran Malinic was the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment's Military Police Battalion. They were in Nova Kasaba, and that particularly on the 13th of July that Bosnian Muslims who were surrendering in that area were being assembled at the football pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was Mr. Malinic in that case able to see them and able to speak with them? Was he able to see the crews and the Muslims surrendering in Nova Kasaba? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that what Mr. Malinic could and did see is outlined in his statement. I am not confirming or refuting any of that with respect to Colonel Malinic, or then Major Malinic, says he saw or did not see. Your question was my awareness of the rationale behind General Mladic approving the use of cameras to film prisoners in Nova Kasaba if, at the same time, General Mladic was aware that the prisoners were going to be killed or had given the order to be killed, and my answer goes back to: I can't explain that rationale, why he did it or what he was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If someone went about creating a plan of crimes, would that individual then bring over journalists to interview the same individuals that he intends to commit crime against and to make a media release on the 13th informing the general public of the presence of prisoners there. Is that a logical way of proceeding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am kind of perplexed as how to answer that. Based on my experience with the OTP in this case, as well as my present experience, logically you would never want to have -- if you were committing a war crime, you would never want to have people around with videotapes and other forms of media to take pictures, and yet they are. I suspect with respect to the VRS media people, the press media people, they knew that any footage that they shot would be subject to censorship by the military, in fact, they were the military media, and that regardless of whatever footage they were to take, that at some point in time a further decision would be made as to what footage ultimately became public. I am not aware that -- while I am aware that Colonel Milutinovic and his VRS camera crew did do extensive videotaping in and around the Srebrenica areas to include those roads on the 12th and the 13th, I am not aware that very much, if any, of the actual footage that they shot has ever been publicly released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at D49. I don't know if we plan to resume -- to adjourn earlier today or if I can still show you the document and I can put my question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may -- we should finish the examination of the witness 20 minutes before 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What we see here is a telegram sent from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade in Rogatica to the Main Staff, personally to General Gvero. The document is entitled: "Accomodation of prisoners of war," and it is signed by assistant commander Major General Zdravko Tolimir. In the upper right-hand corner we tell that it was submitted on the 13th of July, 1995, at 2230 hours. And we are now reading the body of text. "If you are unable to find adequate accomodation for all prisoners of war from Srebrenica, we hereby inform you that room has been found and arranged for 800 prisoners of war in Sjemec in the premises of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade." This is my question: If General Tolimir sent this telegram out on the 13th of July, 1995, at 10.30 p.m., is it possible that he drafted the telegram based on the TV footage that he viewed and upon seeing prisoners of war at the football pitch, therefore suggesting alternative accomodation for these prisoners? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For that proposition to be true, one has to assume first of all that on the evening of 13 July, or at some point as you mention on the 13 July, the television footage from the Nova Kasaba pitch was publicly released and was being aired on the television. I don't know that that's the case. Second, in light of your position as the head of intelligence and security for the entire army, the idea that your primary source of information with regard to the capturing of thousands of prisoners would not be from your own military channels and conversations with various intelligence and security people in and around that whole area but would be off of the basis of a news report. I just don't see that proposition making sense that that's your basis for writing this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Butler. Since your assumptions may be right, as you say, whereas these documents are not necessarily correct - and I indicated the time - would General Tolimir write this document if he had known about the so-called plan of execution at 2232 hours?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be clear, this particular document has -- has a transmission stamp of 2230 hours. It's not evident within the actual document when you actually would have drafted this document. You would have written this document if you were aware of the plan to execute the prisoners, but not necessarily aware yet that it had already been decided that for various reasons that the prisoners would be going to the Zvornik area rather than other locations. So I hold open the possibility that at the point in time that you are writing this proposal about housing prisoners at that location that decisions that are being made with respect to other suitable locations are being made and that you have not yet been informed of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We'll come back to those decisions later. Just tell me what would be adequate accomodation for prisoners of war, and does that mean their execution or does it mean placing them into residential facilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've previously testified, placing them in residential facilities is but one step. There are other actions that need to take place, for example, troops need to be identified to guard the prisoners, food, medicine, and other life support has to be identified and then brought to the location where the prisoners are so they can be food -- can be provided with food, water, and necessary medical care, as many prisoners taken at Srebrenica or the follow days afterwards would have required medical care. So it's a number of steps. And again, when one looks at these locations and tries to make a determination what the point of putting these prisoners at a various location was, that is why I look at more than simply, you know, is it a suitable building as opposed to just a field. If the intent is to properly care for the prisoners within the best ability of the VRS to do so in compliance of the law, there are other things that have to take place for that to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is it possible to continue with this important issue on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. Mr. Butler, this is all that we have for you this week, but regrettably we have to continue on Monday in the afternoon, 2.15 in this courtroom. Now you are free to leave the courtroom. Please be informed that on Tuesday there is an UN holiday. We have no hearing on Tuesday next week.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Goodbye, and have a good weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to go to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One last question. Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber by Mr. Cubbon has sent an e-mail to the Defence on the 2nd of August, 2011, and has asked whether you are able to give us an update about your plans in relation to a possible 98 bis submission. I would like to invite you to update us about your plans on Monday, at the beginning of the hearing on Monday, because it is essential for the Prosecution and the Chamber, and they are preparing work for such a possible submission. It would be very helpful if you can provide us with your intentions. Thank you. This concludes the hearing of today. We adjourn and will resume on Monday, 2.15, in this courtroom.
